description: Hi everyone, we are Team Akula, an inspired squad of students interested in all field of science and we are happy to take part in this competition!
summary:
Agricultural outcomes are heavily dependent on the weather. Cold snaps, dry seasons, and abnormal precipitations are often hard to manually predict, but cause large damages at all levels. Our XGBoost model aims to predict anomalies in weather to give farmers the opportunity to make informed decisions.
As proof of concept, we considered that plants need three essential resources: water through precipitation, adequate temperature and soil moisture. These features are predicted by dedicated XGBoost features. These models are light, fast and flexible enough where each farmer can easily access them. Additionally, for weathers with high variability, farmers may also train specific models for the task with their raw data. We also provided a recommendation table with growth rates. The accuracy of the model decreases with extrapolated time. Plants that reach maturity faster will have a higher probability of benefiting from the predicted weather.
details: Variations in weather can be predicted based on past data: winter is colder than summer, spring and autumn have similar precipitation levels, etc. These indices can be used to train machine learning models where they predict whether the upcoming season is going to present any statistical anomalies compared to previous years. These predictions allow individuals in agricultural backgrounds to make more informed decisions. To achieve this goal, one XGBoost model was trained on a Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) dataset; the PRISM weather data and  NASA POWER data were combined to form a precipitation-temperature dataset. Data from the North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) was injected in the last dataset to prevent overfitting and to provide a wider range of values for XGBoost to pool from. Our findings show that our proposed model is able to identify long term patterns having an MAE in the range of 5% to 10% of the expected value. For more random patterns such as surface moisture, the model struggles to predict its sporadic nature.
